newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazilian pension funds poised for rapid growth.
newsitem.headline: Brazilian pension funds poised for rapid growth.

text.p: Spurred by increased savings, pension funds in Brazil are poised to grow rapidly over the next few years and play a much greater role in local financial markets, analysts said.
With inflation tamed, Brazilians are thinking about the future and saving money, realizing the nation's bankrupt social security system can no longer offer them a smooth transition to retirement.

"Pension funds have an enormous potential growth. Our pension fund industry is just beginning to be explored," said Claudio Munhoz, a director at Previ, the fund for government bank Banco do Brasil's employees and Brazil's largest pension fund.
Munhoz said pension fund assets are estimated to rise to around $200 billion by 2010, from $70 billion today.
He said Brazil still ranks low among nations with developed pension fund sectors in terms of the number of funds and assets as a percentage of GDP.

Brazil has only 350 pension funds, covering nearly two million workers, compared with 750,000 covering about 80 million employees in the United States, home to the world's biggest pension fund system.
Pension funds represent 10.3 percent of Brazil's GDP, while they account for over 30 percent in Chile, the Latin American country that has done most to develop its pension fund industry.

But, with Brazil's ongoing economic stabilization drive on track, this participation could double in five years, said Carlos Garcia Lorenzo Filho, a director at Rio de Janeiro-based investment bank Banco Icatu.
Pension fund growth also depends on changes in legislation to allow more funds to be created. Currently, only private and state companies are allowed to sponsor pension funds.
"Today we cannot have a pension fund for teachers or worker unions as you see in the United States," Lorenzo Filho said.

Last December the federal government began to facilitate the constitution of new pension funds by freeing sponsors from making an initial deposit equivalent to 7.0 percent of their payroll when a new fund is created.
Analysts also said the pension funds will expand independently from the social security reform under discussion in Congress.
Even though the pension and other reforms are held up in Congress, the main idea of the social security proposal is clear -- cutting benefits because the state cannot pay the bills.
Although still small when compared with other countries, Brazil's pension fund industry, which began to expand in the 1970s, saw its assets grow sharply over the past two years.
In 1996, pension fund assets rose 17.5 percent to $69.3 billion over the previous year.
Of this total, $8 billion were return on investments and $2.3 billion were contributions minus retirement payments.
For 1997, the funds' assets are projected to grow by 12 percent, according to estimates by Abrapp, the Brazilian association of pension funds.
Last year the local funds showed a return on assets of 13.4 percent, up from 0.7 percent in 1995, far above their needs to meet retirement payments.
Pension funds are key investors in local financial markets but they are not allowed to invest abroad.

According to the latest Abrapp data collected at the end of October, they held 30.7 percent of their assets in stocks, followed by 16.2 percent in investment funds, mainly fixed income funds, and 13.3 percent in real estate.
Abrapp estimates fixed income investments to have reached $11.2 billion at the end of last year, with investments in public securities totalling $4.4 billion.

Domestic pension funds also have played a major role in Brazil's privatizations. Between 1991, when the country's selloff program started, and 1995, the funds accounted for 16.8 percent of the total revenues raised with the sales.

For instance, Previ, which has $18.6 billion in assets, has participated in most of the country's major privatizations by acquiring stakes in steel firms Usiminas, CSN, Acesita, power utilities Escelsa and Light, and aircraft maker Embraer.
The funds are now getting ready to take part in the upcoming privatizations of state mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce, telecommunications and power sectors.
"We are eyeing all new privatization opportunities," said Previ's Munhoz.
Previ and other funds have joined forces with Bell Canada and banks Opportunity, Citibank and Banco do Brasil to bid for a concession to run Band B cellular services.
